# Nasdaq-100 Multifactor Screen — Executive Research Note

**Methodology reminder:** every score below is a *relative rank inside the Nasdaq-100 this week*. A 70 does not mean "cheap" or "good" — it means "70th percentile of this index, this week." Value scores in particular are cross-sectional ranks on normalised-earnings multiples, not verdicts on valuation. Where `beneficio_en_pico` (earnings-at-peak) is true, treat reported profitability as a cycle reading, not a steady-state one — the multiple looks lowest exactly when the numerator is most inflated. Where `cobertura_pct` (data coverage) is materially below the ~90%+ norm in this set, the score is resting on a thinner evidentiary base. This is research commentary only — no buy/sell/hold view and no position sizing is implied.

---

## 1. SNDK — Sandisk Corporation (score 82.4, cobertura 88%)
**Carries the score:** growth (97.0) and momentum (99.3) are essentially maxed out — 12-month return of ~1,838% and a price 58% above its 200-day average are extreme even for this list. Quality (69.9) is genuinely solid (ROIC 73%, negative accruals, net cash position).
**Drags:** value (47.1) is mid-pack — not a value name.
**Reliability check:** `beneficio_en_pico = true`, and the gap between trailing PER (22.1) and normalised PER (137.1) is the largest sign in this batch that current profitability is a cyclical (NAND/flash-memory upcycle) spike rather than a run-rate. The momentum is real and current, but a two-factor (growth+momentum) story sitting on top of cyclically inflated earnings is a different proposition from a four-factor one. Coverage at 88% is reasonable, not full.

## 2. WDC — Western Digital Corporation (score 75.4, cobertura 81%)
**Carries the score:** growth (88.9) and momentum (88.9), both strong; quality (59.5) is mid.
**Drags:** value (51.6) is unremarkable; balance-sheet leverage (debt/equity 13.4x) is high for the group.
**Reliability check:** `beneficio_en_pico = true` with the same storage-cycle dynamic as Sandisk — normalised PER (69.75) is more than 4x the trailing PER (16.6), implying today's earnings are well above the multi-year base. Recent coverage flags sector-wide profit-taking in storage/semiconductor names tied to AI-demand and rate concerns, which is consistent with a momentum factor that could be more fragile than its current score suggests. Coverage is the lowest of the storage trio (81%).

## 3. NVDA — NVIDIA Corporation (score 72.3, cobertura 94%)
**Carries the score:** growth (95.6) and expectativas (100.0) — the reverse-DCF read is the most favourable in the index this week, alongside genuinely delivered normalised earnings/revenue growth (236%/197%). Quality (62.0) is respectable (huge margins, low leverage, enormous interest coverage).
**Drags:** value (22.4) is the weakest of its five factors — a low rank on normalised multiples in this index; momentum (64.3) is only middling, well below the storage/AMD names, with the stock trading close to its 50-day average.
**Reliability check:** `beneficio_en_pico = true`. This is the broadest-based score in the list (five factors reported, four solid-to-excellent), but the very high expectativas rank should be read carefully: it reflects what the price implies against multi-year delivered growth, not a guarantee that growth continues. Coverage is good (94%).

## 4. STX — Seagate Technology Holdings (score 71.3, cobertura 94%)
**Carries the score:** growth (91.3) and momentum (93.6) dominate.
**Drags:** value (16.9) is the weakest value rank in the entire top ten; quality (60.0) is middling despite a very high headline ROE, which is itself a leverage artefact.
**Reliability check:** `beneficio_en_pico = true`, and the normalised-vs-trailing PER gap (169 vs 59.9) is extreme, again a storage-cycle signature. Debt/equity of ~180x is the highest in the list by a wide margin and materially raises balance-sheet risk under any earnings normalisation. External commentary found in search flags a valuation premium versus storage peers and insider selling — both are worth noting as independent corroboration of the value-factor weakness, not new facts being introduced here. A two-factor (growth+momentum) score sitting on the group's highest leverage and lowest value rank is a fragile combination.

## 5. AMD — Advanced Micro Devices (score 69.2, cobertura 94%)
**Carries the score:** momentum (96.3) and growth (84.9) — the standout is a 12-month return of ~232% and price 49% above the 200-day average.
**Drags:** value (20.5) is weak; quality (55.2) is the softest among the semiconductor peer set here — ROIC of just 5.1% and ROA of 5.1% are low relative to the double-digit-to-high-double-digit returns on capital posted by SNDK, WDC, NVDA and MU.
**Reliability check:** `beneficio_en_pico = true`. The trailing PER (131.7) is already high, and the normalised PER (416.9) is the single largest normalisation gap in the whole list — a strong signal that reported earnings are well above the multi-year earnings power of the business. Momentum here is almost entirely doing the work; quality does not corroborate it.

## 6. DDOG — Datadog, Inc. (score 69.1, cobertura 94%)
**Carries the score:** momentum (84.9), expectativas (85.7) and growth (84.3) are all strong.
**Drags:** value (14.6) is the second-lowest in the top ten; quality (59.0) is a mid score built on low leverage and favourable accruals rather than on returns on capital — ROA is essentially zero (0.18%) and ROIC is 2.5%.
**Reliability check:** `beneficio_en_pico = false` — unusual in this list, meaning current profitability is not being flagged as a cycle peak, but that is largely because profitability is still marginal in absolute terms (thin ROE/ROA). The normalised PER (1,096) versus trailing PER (433.75) shows the earnings base is tiny and volatile. Search results note the stock fell sharply on a results day despite an earnings beat and raised guidance — a concrete illustration of how much growth the market already demands, consistent with the expectativas factor being the story here rather than current profitability.

## 7. MU — Micron Technology (score 68.9, cobertura 94%)
**Carries the score:** momentum (98.0, the highest in the list) and growth (89.2).
**Drags:** quality (45.9) is the weakest of the four "storage cycle" names (SNDK/WDC/STX/MU); value (20.3) is weak.
**Reliability check:** `beneficio_en_pico = false`, which sits oddly next to a normalised-PER gap of 362 vs a trailing PER of 22 and a reported normalised-profit growth rate of 605% — together these numbers point to a business coming out of a deep down-cycle trough rather than one at a stable run-rate, so the earnings-quality caveat that applies to the peak-flagged peers should be applied here too, just via a different mechanism (a depressed multi-year base rather than an inflated current year).

## 8. CRWD — CrowdStrike Holdings (score 68.6, cobertura 75%)
**Carries the score:** momentum (90.6) and expectativas (92.9) are very high; growth (79.8) is solid.
**Drags:** value (16.3) is weak; quality (50.9) is a mid score that masks negative core profitability — operating margin (-2.06%), ROIC (-1.15%) and interest coverage (-3.53) are all negative; normalised profit is negative and no normalised PER can be computed.
**Reliability check:** `cobertura_pct = 75%` is the lowest in this whole list — this score rests on materially partial data and should be weighted accordingly. Search coverage does show constructive sell-side commentary (an Outperform initiation, sector commentary linking cybersecurity to AI infrastructure spend) and record highs for the stock, which is consistent with the momentum/expectativas read, but none of this offsets the fact that the underlying quality inputs are currently negative.

## 9. DXCM — DexCom, Inc. (score 68.4, cobertura 94%)
**Carries the score:** the most evenly distributed profile in the top ten — quality (70.7), expectativas (71.4), growth (75.9), value (48.1) and momentum (68.0) are all positive and none is extreme in either direction.
**Drags:** none dominate; this is the only name in the list without a single factor above ~76 or below ~48.
**Reliability check:** `beneficio_en_pico = true`, so the same cyclical-peak caveat applies to reported profitability, but the normalised PER (54.6) versus trailing PER (32.8) gap is far smaller than for the semiconductor/storage names, suggesting less earnings-cycle distortion. One point worth flagging independently of the score: RSI of 18.6 indicates the shares are technically oversold in the very short term, alongside a much lower 12-month return (9.25%) than every other name on this list — the medium-term momentum score does not fully capture this recent weakness.

## 10. NBIS — Nebius Group N.V. (score 66.7, cobertura 81%)
**Carries the score:** growth (100.0) and momentum (91.9) are both at or near the top of the index.
**Drags:** quality (23.8) and value (23.5) are both weak — among the lowest quality scores in the top ten.
**Reliability check:** the underlying numbers are the most extreme in the list — negative ROA (-1.92%), negative normalised profit, FCF yield of -15.75%, free-cash-flow conversion of -227%, net debt/EBITDA of 8.35x and interest coverage of only 1.22x. The reported 1,284% normalised revenue growth reflects growth off a very small base rather than a mature growth rate, and no expectativas factor could even be computed (likely because normalised earnings are negative). `beneficio_en_pico = true` alongside negative normalised profit is itself notable — "peak" here may simply mean "least negative" rather than "profitable." Coverage at 81% means this score also rests on a partial data set. Search results independently flag "execution risk" tied to a specific facility and note the share price is up over 100% year-to-date, which is consistent with a story where the market is pricing in a great deal of future delivery against a currently unprofitable, high-leverage base.

---

## Closing Ranking by Conviction

Ordering by how well the underlying data corroborates each score — i.e., how many factors genuinely support it, whether reported earnings look cyclically inflated or deflated, how much leverage sits behind the return metrics, and how complete the data coverage is — produces a different order from the raw score ranking:

1. **DXCM** — most broad-based profile (five positive factors, none extreme), smallest earnings-normalisation gap of the peak-flagged names.
2. **SNDK** — genuinely broad strength (growth, momentum, quality), but the earnings-peak/normalisation gap is the largest of the "clean" storage names.
3. **NVDA** — four-to-five factor support and full coverage, held back only by a weak value rank and middling momentum; the very high expectativas rank warrants caution rather than comfort.
4. **WDC** — same storage-cycle earnings caveat as Sandisk, with higher leverage and lower coverage.
5. **MU** — momentum-led, weakest quality of the storage cohort, and a normalisation gap that likely reflects a low prior-year base as much as current strength.
6. **AMD** — momentum dominates over a quality profile (ROIC ~5%) that is the softest among the large semiconductor names here, with the single largest normalised-PER gap in the list.
7. **STX** — highest leverage in the index by a wide margin and the weakest value rank, sitting under a momentum/growth-led score; independent commentary flags a valuation premium versus peers.
8. **DDOG** — momentum/expectativas-led score over near-zero return-on-capital metrics; a large earnings reaction in recent results underscores how much is already priced in.
9. **CRWD** — momentum/expectativas-led score over negative operating profitability, and the lowest data-coverage figure in the entire list (75%), meaning the score itself is the least complete.
10. **NBIS** — the most concentrated score (growth and momentum only), sitting on the weakest quality profile in the top ten, negative free cash flow, elevated leverage, and only partial data coverage (81%).

**Where this disagrees with the raw score order:** the score order places SNDK, WDC, STX, AMD and MU (in that sequence) ahead of DXCM and NVDA largely on the strength of momentum and growth. Conviction-adjusted, DXCM and NVDA move up because their scores are corroborated by more factors and cleaner (or fuller) data, while STX and AMD move down because their scores lean most heavily on momentum and growth alone, sit on top of the group's weakest quality/leverage readings, and carry the largest gaps between reported and normalised earnings. CRWD and NBIS remain at the bottom in both orderings, but the conviction view puts more weight on their reliance on partial data (CRWD) and negative return-on-capital/cash-flow metrics (NBIS) than the raw score alone conveys.

methodology.approach: Factor scoring, not threshold filtering. Every company in the index is ranked against every other on each metric, and the ranks are combined with the weights below. Nothing is rejected for scoring poorly — only for being impossible to evaluate.
methodology.why_not_filters: A hard filter chain (ROE > 20% AND P/E < 20 AND ...) discards a company at 19.8% ROE as readily as one at 3%, empties the screen when no name clears every bar, throws away how far each company cleared or missed, and silently gives RSI the same weight as ROE. A cross-sectional rank has none of those problems.
methodology.why_ranks_not_values: Scores are built from percentile ranks rather than raw values. One company emerging from a cyclical trough at +1,368% earnings growth would otherwise dominate any average and turn a multi-factor score into a single column in disguise. A rank treats that as what it is — first place — and nothing more.

growth.what_it_measures: How fast revenue and earnings are compounding, measured against a multi-year base rather than a single prior year — a comparison against one weak year is arithmetic, not growth.

quality.what_it_measures: Whether the business earns its returns on real capital and turns profit into cash. Accruals and leverage sit here because both are ways a good-looking profit can fail to be one.

momentum.what_it_measures: Whether the price agrees. Deliberately the lowest weight in the value screens: a company that has fallen is cheaper, not worse, and momentum should not be able to veto it.

value.what_it_measures: What you pay for what the business earns and owns. Built on normalised earnings rather than the last twelve months, so a company at the top of its cycle does not read as cheap.

expectativas.what_it_measures: How much growth today's price already demands, from the reverse DCF, against what the business has actually delivered. It is the only factor that scores the market's expectations rather than the company.

methodology.missing_data: A metric a company does not report scores nothing — never zero. Scoring a gap as the worst possible value punishes a company for a data provider's omission, and that is the kind of error that never appears in the table and decides the order anyway. A factor is averaged over the metrics that exist, and the weights are renormalised over the factors that exist.
methodology.coverage: Because weights renormalise, a company with thin data scores as confidently as a complete one. cobertura_pct is published alongside every score for exactly that reason: 90 on 40% coverage is an opinion about very little.
methodology.what_the_score_is_not: The score is a position within this index, not a grade and not a valuation. A company's score moves when other companies move. It says nothing about whether the name is worth owning, and it is not a recommendation.
methodology.read_the_breakdown: The per-factor scores matter more than the total. 'Cheap and high quality but no momentum' is a statement you can argue with; a composite of 67 is not.
methodology.two_stage: Four factors are ranked across the whole index (100 companies). The fifth, expectativas, comes from a reverse DCF that reads SEC filings and cannot run at that scale, so the top 25 are valued and ranked on it among themselves. The other four keep their index-wide percentile — re-ranking them inside an already-selected group would measure something different and read as if it did not.
methodology.report_size: The 10 highest-scoring companies go into the written report. That number is chosen rather than whatever a threshold happened to admit, which is what makes the cost of the run predictable.

valuation_method.model: Two-stage DCF on levered free cash flow (FCF discounted at cost of equity, compared with market cap — no net-debt bridge)
valuation_method.discount_rate: CAPM: currency-matched risk-free rate + beta x 5% ERP, beta clamped to [0.3, 2.5], rate clamped to [5%, 18%]. Only USD has a live quote (^TNX); other currencies use a documented static rate, flagged per company in risk_free_source.
valuation_method.implied_growth: Reverse DCF — the FCF growth rate that sets the model's equity value equal to today's market cap. What the price assumes, not a forecast. Available for every company, since it needs no history.
valuation_method.trend_test: A projection is only made when a least-squares line through log FCF reaches R2 >= 0.5. Below that the series is a path rather than a direction, dcf_value_per_share is null and dcf_skipped_reason says so.
valuation_method.probability: P(growth >= implied growth) under a Student-t fitted to the company's own year-on-year FCF growth in log space. Withheld entirely above a log stdev of 1.0, where it would be indistinguishable from a coin flip.
known_limits: History depth is uneven. SEC filings give US companies 14-17 years (16 growth observations for Adobe), but that source only covers SEC filers, so the IBEX screener and any company whose filing history has gaps falls back to yfinance's 4 years — 3 observations. Each company's fcf_source and probability.observations say which it got, and every probability is published as a range rather than a point.

A short FCF window can catch a trough, a spike or both and mistake it for a trend, and a long one can fit an earlier version of the company beautifully. The R2 test guards the first, and projecting the lower of the long-run and recent trends guards the second. Neither is a cure.
Terminal growth is a single 2.5% applied to every business regardless of its long-run ceiling; dcf_terminal_value_share_pct shows how much of each valuation rests on it.

The model sees free cash flow only — no revenue detail, margins, guidance or segments. A one-off legal settlement, licensing payment or deferred capex is indistinguishable from a genuine trend change, which is why revenue growth is carried alongside as a corroboration check.
Levered FCF is compared directly against market cap with no net-debt bridge — a deliberate simplification for data robustness across 500 tickers.

valuation_report:
# What Today's Price Is Assuming — A Reverse-DCF Read Across the Nasdaq-100 Quality Screen

The number that matters most here is `implied_growth_pct`: the FCF growth rate a company would have to sustain, compounded over ten years plus a 2.5% terminal perpetuity, to justify today's market cap. Everything else — trend, history, probability — exists to answer a single question: has this company's own cash-flow record ever behaved anything like that number, and how often?

---

## 1. Companies whose cash flows are trend-like enough to compare (trend R² ≥ 0.5)

For these names, `trend_growth_pct` is a legitimate least-squares read on the whole series, so the gap between it and `implied_growth_pct` is evidence, not arithmetic. A negative gap (implied − trend) means the price assumes deceleration from the historical trend; a positive gap means the price assumes acceleration beyond it.

**FTNT** — Price assumes 23.1% FCF growth. Trend R²=0.977 is the strongest fit in the set, with realized trend growth of 26.4% — the price is actually assuming a *slight slowdown* (gap −3.3pp) from a historical trend that has been unusually clean. A full DCF was produced: $93.83/share, −39.9% versus the current $156.07, with 62% of that value sitting in the terminal-year perpetuity. Probability of clearing 23.1% growth: 48.5%, banded 48.2–48.8% on 13 observations — essentially a coin flip against its own history.

**AMD** — Trend R²=0.611, trend growth 41.5%, but the *implied* growth is null: `above_model_range`, meaning the growth the market needs exceeds even the reverse solver's search range. A forward DCF was still built using the capped trend growth of 8.5%, producing $18.16/share versus a $516.13 price (−96.5%), with 32% terminal weight. Read together: even a generous, trend-consistent projection falls far short of price, and the actual required growth is higher still — the model has nothing further to say about how much higher. No probability could be assigned (reason: implied growth above model range).

**DXCM** — Trend R²=0.729, but historical growth was capped and the growth that would need to be projected (68.6%) sits outside the model's usable band [−15%, 25%], so no DCF value was produced — that null is the finding, not an omission. Implied growth of 22.3% is available and sits well inside the trend (gap −46.3pp), i.e., the market is pricing something far tamer than the recent trend has shown. Revenue growth (17%) vs. FCF trend growth (68.6%) diverges by 51.6pp — a flag that FCF has been moving faster than the topline, for reasons this data cannot identify. No probability could be estimated: log-stdev of 1.84 was judged too volatile for any figure to mean something.

**NVDA** — Trend R²=0.903 on a still-short (4-year) series. Trend growth of 186% dwarfs the 40.8% the market is actually pricing in (gap −145pp) — the price assumes a dramatic deceleration from the recent run-rate, which is itself unsurprising given how extreme that run-rate is. Growth outside the usable band meant no DCF value was produced. Probability of the required 40.8% given NVDA's own (extremely short) history: 77.7%, banded 70.3–90.0% on just 3 observations — a wide band that should be read as "this specific pace of growth has usually been cleared in the very few years on record," not as a forecast.

**DDOG** — Trend R²=0.819, trend growth 94.0% vs. implied 35.1% (gap −58.9pp): the price assumes a steep slowdown from the recent trend. Growth outside the modelled band meant DCF was skipped. Probability: 70.5%, range 66.0–78.0% on 6 observations.

**MRVL** — Trend R²=0.813, trend growth 19.5% vs. implied 51.9% (gap +32.4pp) — here the price is assuming *acceleration* well beyond the historical trend, the opposite pattern from most of the group. A DCF using the (in-band) trend growth of 19.5% produced $31.36/share vs. $236.10 (−86.7%), with 46% terminal weight — underscoring how far the market's implied growth sits above what the trend itself would support. Probability of the modelled 19.5% given the company's own volatility: 22.5%, range 12.0–29.1% on only 4 observations — a low band, but on a very thin sample.

**DASH** — Trend R²=0.746, trend growth 74.3% vs. implied 27.0% (gap −47.3pp): price assumes substantial deceleration. DCF skipped (growth outside band). No probability estimate: log-stdev 1.22 flagged too volatile.

**PLTR** — Trend R²=0.823, trend growth 74.8% vs. implied 54.8% (gap −19.9pp): still assumes deceleration, but a smaller one than most peers here. DCF skipped (growth outside band). Probability: 51.5%, range 51.1–52.6% on 4 observations — essentially a coin flip, tightly banded only because the sample is small.

**CRWD** — Trend R²=0.716, trend growth 105.7% vs. implied 42.2% (gap −63.5pp) — one of the largest assumed slowdowns in the set. DCF skipped (growth outside band). No probability: log-stdev 1.10, too volatile.

**MSFT** — Trend R²=0.885, trend growth 8.7% vs. implied 21.9% (gap +13.2pp): price assumes *acceleration* above a well-behaved, decade-plus trend. DCF: $121.59/share vs. $495.63 (−75.5%), 47% terminal weight. Probability of hitting 21.9% given 16 years of Microsoft's own growth history: 17.7%, range 13.0–21.6% — the most data-supported band in the set, and it says this pace has rarely been cleared.

**LRCX** — Trend R²=0.882, trend growth 19.1% vs. implied 35.6% (gap +16.4pp): price assumes acceleration. DCF: $79.07 vs. $298.22 (−73.5%), 48% terminal weight. Probability: 32.3%, range 28.6–34.9% on 15 observations.

**VRTX** — Trend R²=0.866, trend growth 32.5% vs. implied 14.8% (gap −17.7pp): price assumes deceleration from a trend that has itself been erratic (note the discount rate here rests on a beta of 0.32, giving a 6.57% cost of equity — below the general 7% floor described for this model, flagged as-is from the data rather than reconciled). DCF: $216.32 vs. $515.44 (−58.0%), with a striking 69.3% of value from the terminal perpetuity — the highest share in the group, meaning most of this valuation rests on the single 2.5% assumption rather than the ten explicit years. Probability: 71.0%, range 66.9–77.2% on 8 observations.

**META** — Trend R²=0.797, trend growth 33.8% vs. implied 17.6% (gap −16.2pp): price assumes deceleration. DCF: $610.25 vs. $648.03 (−5.8%, the smallest gap to price in the set), 58% terminal weight. Probability: 62.5%, range 60.4–65.5% on 13 observations.

**GOOGL / GOOG** — Same underlying company (Alphabet), two share classes, same cash-flow series (trend R²=0.903, trend growth 17.4%). GOOGL: implied 24.7% (gap +7.3pp); GOOG: implied 24.5% (gap +7.2pp) — both assume mild acceleration above trend, the small difference reflecting the price gap between classes. DCF values differ correspondingly: $159.62 (−52.8%) for GOOGL, $169.45 (−49.5%) for GOOG, both ~46% terminal weight. Probability essentially identical: ~38%, range roughly 34.6–40.4% on 10 observations.

**BKR** — Trend R²=0.567 (the weakest fit that still clears the bar), trend growth 22.7% vs. implied 11.5% (gap −11.2pp): price assumes a large deceleration. This is the one company in the set where the DCF value exceeds price: $113.38 vs. $59.06, +92.0% upside, though 67% of that value is terminal-perpetuity-driven — a large share of a positive result resting on the same fixed 2.5% assumption used everywhere else. Probability: 52.9%, range 52.3–54.1% on 7 observations.

---

## 2. Companies where the model declined to compare (trend R² < 0.5, or too little data)

For these, the cash-flow series does not behave like a trend — either R² is too low, or there are too few usable points. `implied_growth_pct` (where computable) is reported on its own, without a trend comparison, because there is nothing reliable to compare it to. That silence is the finding.

**SNDK** — Implied growth 23.95%, priced off only four data points (three deeply negative, then a jump to $11.5bn FCF). Not enough usable points to fit a trend; no historical CAGR, no trend growth. Beta was missing and defaulted to 1.0. Probability: no usable estimate — fewer than two year-on-year growth observations exist. The price assumes 24% compounding growth off a base that has essentially no track record behind it.

**WDC** — Implied growth 45.93%. Trend R²=0.016 — the series is a path, not a direction (endpoint CAGR of 6.9% and trend "growth" of −2.0% point in opposite ways, which itself confirms there is no direction to read). Revenue grew 27.3% against a slightly negative FCF trend, a 29.3pp divergence that could reflect capex timing, working capital, or something else — this data cannot say which. DCF was skipped outright. The Student-t probability model, which runs on year-on-year growth dispersion rather than trend fit, still produced a result: 35.4%, range 31.9–37.8% on 13 observations — worth reporting, but it says only that this pace of growth has been cleared roughly a third of the time historically, not that the trend supports it.

**STX** — Implied growth 45.33%. Trend R²=0.04, equally directionless. Revenue grew 18.2% against a −2.3% FCF trend (−20.5pp divergence). DCF skipped. Probability: 34.1%, range 30.7–36.5% on 15 observations.

**ARM** — Implied growth is null (`above_model_range`) — the market's required growth exceeds the solver's range entirely. Trend R²=0.009. Beta was clamped from a reported 3.89 down to the model ceiling, pushing the discount rate to 17.5%. No probability was computed, because the input it would depend on (implied growth) doesn't exist here.

**LITE** — Implied growth null (`above_model_range`). Trend R²=0.272 — recent growth (10.1%) and full-period trend (30.7%) disagree, another sign the series isn't behaving consistently. No historical CAGR (an unstable early base makes the endpoint calculation invalid). No probability computed, for the same above-range reason as ARM.

**ALAB** — Implied growth null (`above_model_range`). Only four years of data and not enough usable points even to attempt a trend. Beta clamped from a reported 3.78 to 2.5. Only one year-on-year growth observation exists, precluding any probability estimate independent of the above-range issue.

---

## 3. Reading the probability figures honestly

Every probability above is a Student-t estimate fitted to a company's own historical year-on-year log growth — typically on well under 20 data points, often under 10. Treat the *range*, not the point estimate, as the answer: a range like MSFT's 13.0–21.6% or NVDA's 70.3–90.0% is already an admission of how much uncertainty a handful of annual observations carries. A high band (VRTX, NVDA, DDOG, CRWD-adjacent names, DASH) says this company's own history has often produced growth at or above the rate the market now needs — it is a statement about the past frequency of a pattern, not a forecast that the pattern continues. A low band (MSFT, MRVL) says the required growth has been rare in that company's own record. Where `probability_pct` is null, that is not a low probability — it is a refusal to estimate, either because there aren't enough usable observations (SNDK), the growth series is too volatile to trust a Student-t fit (DXCM, DASH, CRWD, log-stdev > 1.0), or the implied growth itself was never computable (AMD, ARM, LITE, ALAB).

---

## 4. Where this model is most likely wrong

- **The sample size behind every probability.** Most of these estimates rest on well under 20 annual observations, and several — NVDA (3), MRVL (4), PLTR (4), DDOG (6), AMD (6) — rest on fewer than 10. A Student-t distribution fitted to 3–6 points cannot meaningfully separate a 40% probability from a 70% one; the wide bands quoted above are the honest expression of that, not a caveat to be waved away.

- **The four-year FCF window in several cases (SNDK, NVDA, ARM, ALAB).** A model that only sees four data points cannot distinguish a structural growth trend from one cycle of a semiconductor or hardware boom. NVDA's 186% trend growth and SNDK's jump from negative to $11.5bn FCF in a single year are exactly the kind of series a longer window would either confirm or dismantle — this model cannot tell which, and says so by refusing several of the downstream calculations.

- **One terminal growth rate (2.5%) applied to every business alike.** Where `dcf_terminal_value_share_pct` is high — VRTX (69%), BKR (67%), FTNT (62%), META (58%) — most of the equity value produced by this model is that single fixed long-run assumption, applied identically to a biotech, an oilfield services company, a cybersecurity vendor and a social media platform. These businesses do not share a long-run ceiling, and the model has no way to differentiate them on that dimension.

- **The model sees cash flow, never the reason for it.** A jump in FCF from a licensing payment, a legal settlement, a deferred capex program, or a one-time working-capital release looks identical in this data to a genuine acceleration in the underlying business. WDC's and STX's near-zero trend R² and large FCF-versus-revenue divergences (−29.3pp and −20.5pp respectively) are consistent with this kind of noise, but this dataset contains no margin, segment, or guidance detail that could confirm or rule it out — that is a limit of what is being measured, not a conclusion about what happened.

This is a description of what current prices imply and how those implications compare with each company's own, often thin, cash-flow record. It is not a projection of what will happen next, and none of the above should be read as a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any of these securities.
